summary: Defines MIB modules for managing Ethernet in the First Mile Copper interfaces, 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL, as specified by IEEE 802.3ah. They extend the existing Ethernet-like interfaces and MAU MIB modules with objects for these copper links. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives network tools a standard way to ask Ethernet-over-copper-wire links how they are doing, such as a dashboard for those lines.

questions: what is a pme in efm
subtitle: A standard SNMP vocabulary for managing Ethernet-over-copper links built from one or more bonded copper pairs.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.3ah defined new Ethernet interfaces over voice-grade copper (2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS) that can bond several copper pairs, but network management software had no standard objects to configure and monitor them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules: EFM-CU-MIB for the copper ports and their per-pair modems, and IF-CAP-STACK-MIB for describing which lower layers a device could connect to which upper layers. It builds on the Interfaces Group, Ethernet-like and MAU MIB modules.
tldr.outcome: Managers can provision, bond and monitor EFM Copper links through SNMP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7124.

today: RFC 5066 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7124. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Ethernet Over Voice-Grade Copper
sections.content:
IEEE Std 802.3ah-2004, known as Ethernet in the First Mile (EFM), defined new Ethernet physical interfaces that run over voice-grade copper pairs. Together they are called EFM Copper (EFMCu). 2BASE-TL is the long-reach PHY, based on SHDSL technology. 10PASS-TS is the short-reach PHY, based on VDSL technology.

2BASE-TL is capable of at least 2 Mbps over a 2700 m single copper pair, and 10PASS-TS of at least 10 Mbps over a 750 m single pair. Both support optional PME aggregation, also called multi-pair bonding, with variable rates.

This memo defines a MIB module for managing these interfaces, plus a second module describing the cross-connect capability of stacked interfaces. Managed objects for the OAM and EPON parts of 802.3ah live in the EFM-COMMON-MIB (RFC 4878) and the EFM-EPON-MIB (RFC 4837).
sections.plainLanguage: Some Ethernet connections run over old phone wires. This document is the instruction sheet that lets control software ask those wires how they are doing.

sections.title: Layering: One Port, Many Modems
sections.content:
An EFMCu port can aggregate up to 32 Physical Medium Entity (PME) devices, which are the individual modems, using the PME Aggregation Function (PAF). On top sits a single Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS) port that connects to the MAC. Each PCS is cross-connected to a number of PMEs, with one PCS per PME.

The MIB maps this onto the Interfaces Group MIB. The PCS and MAC appear as one ifEntry with ifType ethernetCsmacd(6). Each PME appears as its own interface, with ifType shdsl(169) for 2BASE-TL or vdsl(97) for 10PASS-TS. Every PME and PCS MUST have a unique interface index.

For a PME, ifSpeed is the actual data bit rate, and zero while the PME is Initializing or Down. For the PCS it is the sum of the current data rates of all PMEs in the group, without the 64/65-octet encapsulation overhead and PAF overhead, but accounting for Inter-Frame Gaps.

The actual connections are held in ifStackTable and its inverse ifInvStackTable. The new read-only ifCapStackTable and ifInvCapStackTable list which PMEs could possibly be connected to which PCS. To check that a PME can really be attached, a manager SHALL inspect ifCapStackTable, ifStackTable and efmCuPAFCapacity together.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of one big pipe made of several thin straws. The pipe is the port you see, and each straw is one modem on one wire. The tables say which straws could go with which pipe and which ones really do.

sections.title: Bonding, Discovery and Link Startup
sections.content:
The PAF fragments Ethernet frames, sends the fragments over several PMEs, and reassembles the frames at the far port. PAF is OPTIONAL, but the agent is REQUIRED to report the PAF capability for every EFMCu port. Enabling PAF turns on fragmentation and reassembly even on a single-PME port.

Ports may also support discovery. During initialization the PMEs exchange information about their aggregation groups, which can be used to detect copper misconnections or to assign local PMEs to groups automatically. Discovery works only if PAF is supported and enabled. The RFC gives a pseudo-code example of a central-office device claiming remote devices by writing a 6-octet discovery code, and notes that fixed or manual assignment are equally valid.

EFMCu ports need a lengthy training process before data can pass, which may take tens of seconds, especially with PAF. Setting ifAdminStatus to up starts it. A PCS is operationally up if at least one of its PMEs is up, is lowerLayerDown when all PMEs are down, and is notPresent when it has no PME. The MIB expands a PME's down state into downReady, downNotReady and init through efmCuPmeOperStatus.

Removing the last operationally up PME from an up PCS would drop the link entirely, so it is RECOMMENDED that implementations reject it.
sections.plainLanguage: Tying wires together is like several people carrying one long table. Before anyone can carry it, they all have to line up and get ready, and that takes a little while.

sections.title: MIB Structure and PME Profiles
sections.content:
EFM-CU-MIB has two main groups. efmCuPort holds configuration, capability, status and notification objects common to all EFMCu PHYs. efmCuPme holds the same kinds of objects for individual PMEs, and contains efmCuPme2B and efmCuPme10P groups for the two PHY types. The second module, IF-CAP-STACK-MIB, has just the two capability tables.

Setting every parameter on every PHY would be burdensome, so the MIB uses shared configuration profiles. There are 12 predefined standard profiles for 2BASE-TL and 22 for 10PASS-TS, taken from 802.3ah, plus two extra predefined best-effort profiles for 2BASE-TL. New profiles can be defined for specific copper environments and spectral regulations.

A profile is assigned to a PME through efmCuPmeAdminProfile. If that is zero, the efmCuAdminProfile of the connected PCS decides, so one common profile can cover all PMEs with individual overrides. The profile in use is pointed to by efmCuPmeOperProfile, which can be created automatically to reflect parameters achieved in adaptive initialization.

Most objects have no direct counterpart in IEEE Clause 30 and instead refer to Clause 45 registers. The RFC includes a table mapping the Clause 30 attributes to MIB objects, for example aPAFSupported to efmCuPAFSupported and aLocalPAFCapacity to efmCuPAFCapacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of setting every dial on every line, you make a recipe card once and give the same card to many lines. A line can still have its own card if it needs one.

sections.title: Fit With Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
Implementing the Ethernet-like MIB (RFC 3635) and the MAU MIB (RFC 4836) is REQUIRED for EFMCu interfaces. The MAU MIB gained two ifMauType values, dot3MauType2BaseTL and dot3MauType10PassTS, and two ifMauMediaAvailable values, availableReduced and ready. Most MAU characteristics do not apply, since there is no auto-negotiation, false carrier or jabber, but the MAU type tells management software to look in EFM-CU-MIB. PMEs are not Ethernet-like interfaces, so they cannot be MAU objects.

For the aggregated port, ifMauMediaAvailable takes meanings such as available (interface up, all PMEs up) and availableReduced (up, but one or more PMEs report a receive-direction link fault while at least one is up).

The SHDSL (RFC 4319) and VDSL (RFC 4070) MIB modules describe similar modems. The RFC chose not to reference them, for simplicity, shared attributes and consistent names, and defines all relevant objects in EFM-CU-MIB. Groups from those modules, for example performance monitoring, MAY still be included where the PME supports them.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rulebook fits alongside older rulebooks for similar equipment. It borrows from them where it helps and writes its own rules where the old ones did not match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects in EFM-CU-MIB are read-write or read-create, and most are writable only while the link is Down. Careless writes can be disruptive. Changing efmCuPmeAdminSubType may lock the link, because peer PMEs of the same subtype cannot exchange handshake messages. Enabling efmCuPAFAdminState can lock the link if the peer does not support PAF. Changing profiles may degrade the rate or stop initialization altogether, and activating one PME can cause cross-talk that severely degrades another EFMCu PHY.

Readable objects can be sensitive too. Because EFMCu runs over unshielded twisted pair in bundles that may carry other operators' or customers' pairs, it is theoretically possible to eavesdrop on a transmission by listening to cross-talk, especially if the link parameters are known.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its authentication and privacy mechanisms, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the settings on a line is like turning the knobs on a radio: the wrong turn can make everything go silent. So only people you trust should be allowed to turn them, and your messages should be locked.
